The letter of ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ opens with a name and almost nothing else: James, a servant of God and of the Lord ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧. He does not say which James he is, and he does not need to. Several men of that name appear in the New Testament. James the son of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧, one of the twelve, was put to death by King ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ little more than a decade after the crucifixion. The James who wrote this letter is another man altogether: the brother of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.

His is a remarkable story. He grew up in the same household in ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧, one of four brothers named in the Gospels, alongside ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧, ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧ and Judas, the ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ of a later letter. The New Testament calls him the Lord's brother. During ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' ministry, John's Gospel says, his brothers did not believe in him. Then, after the resurrection, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ records that the risen Jesus appeared to ⟦p:james_719|James⟧, and from that point everything changes. In the book of Acts, James becomes the leading figure of the church in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧. When ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ escapes from prison, he asks that word be sent to James. When the apostles meet to decide whether Gentile believers must keep the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, it is James who sums up the matter. Paul calls him one of the pillars of the church. Later tradition remembered him as James the Just, a man of such constant prayer that his knees grew hard as a camel's. The Jewish historian Josephus records his death in the early sixties of the first century: in a gap between Roman governors, the high priest had him stoned.

The letter is addressed to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion. That was the name for the Jewish communities scattered beyond the land of Israel, in ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, ⟦l:mesopotamia_790|Mesopotamia⟧ and ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ itself. ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ is writing to Jewish believers in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ living among them, like those Acts describes as scattered from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ after the death of ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧. The word he uses for their meeting is, in Greek, synagogue. These are ordinary people, many of them poor, some of them labourers whose wages have been withheld, harassed by wealthy men who drag them into court. Within the community there are quarrels, flattery of the rich, careless talk, and traders who plan their profits as if tomorrow were theirs to command.

⟦p:james_719|James⟧ wrote it in the years before his death, and it is among the earliest Christian writings. Its world is plain to see: Jewish, rooted in the Scriptures of Israel, and close to the earliest days of the church.

It reads less like a personal letter than a collection of wisdom. There are no greetings to friends, no news, no travel plans, and no farewell. Instead there are short, sharp sayings and vivid pictures, in the tradition of Proverbs: a wave tossed by the wind, a horse turned by a bit, a ship steered by a small rudder, a forest set ablaze by a spark, a farmer waiting for the rain. Commands come thick and fast. And although ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ names ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ only twice, his words are full of echoes of his brother's teaching, especially the Sermon on the Mount: blessing for those who endure, treasure eaten by moths, a yes that means yes.

The letter does not build a single argument from start to finish. Its subjects circle and return: trials and the wisdom to face them, rich and poor, hearing and doing, the power of the tongue, quarrels, pride and humility. It opens with joy in the middle of trials. It moves through its most famous passage, on faith that shows itself in deeds. It speaks of the tongue and of two kinds of wisdom, of friendship with the world and of plans made without God. And it closes with a fierce warning to the rich, a call to patience until the Lord comes, and a word about prayer for the sick, ending abruptly with a brother brought back from wandering.

⟦p:james_719|James⟧ stands first in a group of letters the early church called general or catholic letters, meaning that they were written not to one congregation but to believers more widely. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, John and ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ follow. Of all of them, James sounds most like the Old Testament prophets and wise men, a voice from the first generation of believers in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, speaking to scattered communities under pressure.
1:
After a single line of greeting to the scattered tribes, ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ goes straight to the hardest thing in his readers' lives: trials of many kinds. In Greek there is a link between the two sentences that English loses, as the ordinary word of greeting gives way at once to a call to consider it pure joy.

The chapter moves the way a wisdom teacher moves, from one saying to the next, often joined by a single word. Trials lead to perseverance, perseverance to maturity, and the thought of lacking anything leads to asking God for wisdom. Brief pictures flash past: a wave driven by the wind, a wild flower withering in the scorching sun. Then ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ turns from the trials that test from outside to the temptations that pull from within, and insists that these do not come from God.

The last part gathers around the word of God, received and then acted on. ⟦p:james_719|James⟧'s picture of a man who glances in a mirror and forgets his own face introduces a concern that will run through the whole letter. The chapter closes with a short definition of true religion, and it points to the care of orphans and widows.
2:
⟦p:james_719|James⟧ now walks his readers into their own gathering. Two visitors arrive at the same moment. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes; the other is poor and shabbily dressed. Who is offered a seat and who is told to stand is a scene James's readers would have recognised. They have been honouring the wealthy, the very people who oppress them and haul them before the courts.

Against this ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ sets what he calls the royal law, the command from Leviticus to love your neighbour as yourself, and a reminder that the law cannot be kept selectively.

That leads into the passage for which the letter is best known. ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ imagines someone who claims to have faith but has nothing to show for it, who wishes a hungry brother well and sends him away empty. He calls such faith dead, and he brings two witnesses from Israel's Scriptures: ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ offering ⟦p:isaac_616|Isaac⟧ on the altar, and ⟦p:rahab_2388|Rahab⟧ of ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, who sheltered the spies. James quotes the same verse from Genesis that ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ uses when he writes of faith. His own target is plain: a faith that never moves beyond words.
3:
Talk of faith that is only words leads ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ to words themselves. He begins with a caution to those who would be teachers in the community, since teachers work with their tongues, and they will be judged more strictly for it.

Then comes a string of images from everyday life. A small bit in a horse's mouth turns the whole animal. A small rudder steers a great ship through strong winds. A small spark sets a whole forest alight. Every kind of creature has been tamed, but no one can tame the tongue. The same mouth blesses God and curses people made in his likeness, and ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ asks whether a spring can pour out fresh water and salt, or a fig tree bear olives.

Back in chapter one, ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ told his readers to ask God for wisdom and to bridle their tongues. Both concerns return here together. The chapter ends by setting two kinds of wisdom side by side, one earthly, bred of jealousy and selfish ambition, the other from above, pure and peace-loving. The bitter rivalry he describes is about to come into the open.
4:
The jealousy and selfish ambition ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ has just described have consequences, and now he names them: conflicts and quarrels within the community. He traces them back to desires at war inside people, to craving what they cannot have, and to prayers that are really requests for more pleasure.

His language becomes sharp and urgent. He calls his readers adulteresses, an image the prophets of Israel had used for a people unfaithful to God, and he sets friendship with the world against friendship with God. Then, quoting the book of Proverbs, he reminds them that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. A rapid run of commands follows, calling them to submit to God, resist ⟦p:satan_2476|the devil⟧, draw near and humble themselves, and to stop slandering and judging one another.

The chapter ends with a new audience. Come now, ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ says, and he turns to the traders among them, who speak confidently of going to a city for a year and making a profit. He reminds them that their lives are like a morning mist.
5:
⟦p:james_719|James⟧'s words to confident merchants turn into something much stronger. Again he says come now, and this time he addresses the rich, with the voice of an Old Testament prophet. Their stored wealth is rotting, their clothes moth-eaten, their gold corroded. The wages they held back from the labourers who harvested their fields are crying out, and the cries have reached the Lord of Hosts. Like the prophets who denounced nations that would never hear them, James speaks over his readers' heads to the wealthy who exploit them.

Then he turns back to his brothers, the poor and the wronged, and calls them to patience until the Lord's coming. His picture is the farmer in the land of Israel, waiting for the autumn and spring rains. He offers the prophets, ⟦p:job_1639|Job⟧ and ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ as examples of endurance and of prayer.

The final paragraphs are practical and gentle: plain speech without oaths, prayer in trouble and song in gladness, and elders called to pray over the sick and anoint them with oil. ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ closes not with greetings but with one last concern, for any who wander from the truth.
